title: Ang 923–924: the Sadd
tomorrow: what if the one you miss was standing close all along?
last: BLISS: THE SONGS AND THE EASE.

cards: A gentle note for families: today's hymn is about a death. Some families gather a playlist for a funeral, the songs the person loved, so the room isn't only silence. Ang 923 holds something close to that: last wishes.
The Sadd, the call, tells of Guru Amar Das when the call came for him to go. He gathers his family and his Sikhs around him. And the first thing he asks for isn't black cloth or a hush.

teach.b: The Sadd is a short poem, set down by a poet named Sundar; tradition says he was of the Guru's own family. In it, the Guru speaks plainly.

teach.h: LET NO ONE WEEP FOR ME.
teach.b: In paraphrase: let no one weep for me after I'm gone; that would not please me at all.
Then what to do instead: sing the praises of the One, call those who read the Lord's story, let kirtan fill the room. He isn't scolding grief. He's turning it.

The tears belong to the people who love him, and he hands them a song to carry that love somewhere. In the same poem he names who comes next: Ram Das, the builder from the platform story, and asks everyone to bow to him.
So the Sadd isn't only an ending.
It's a handover, sung. That's why it's a lesson for the ears. The Sadd lives in sound.
Sikh families often sing kirtan when someone dies, and the Sadd itself is read, the Guru's own request kept as practice. Grief is real here, and nothing pretends it isn't.
But the room is asked to fill with voices, a harmonium, one line sung again and again until the breath steadies. The love stays. It just gets a tune.

how: When a Sikh dies, family and sangat gather for kirtan and a reading of the Granth; the Sadd, Guru Amar Das's request that no one weep for him, is read, and the Anand is sung.

games.q: at a family friend's memorial the room is silent and stiff, and you're asked to help. by the Sadd, what fits?
o: ask someone to begin kirtan, or a song the person loved.
gently ask people to stop crying so the program can go on.
keep it silent; music would make light of the loss.
games.why: the Sadd turns grief toward song: sing the praises of the One, let kirtan fill the room. tears aren't banned; they're given a tune.

practice: Hum one low note on each out-breath, soft enough that only you can hear it. Notice where it buzzes: lips, chest, the bones of the face. If a sad thought comes, let it ride the note out instead of pushing it away.
If you'd like, read the opening of the Sadd on ang 923 first.

wordCard.voice: Ang 923. Where the Sadd stands, the call: Guru Amar Das's last wishes, and a song handed to the people who'd grieve him.

carryVoice: Sing, don't weep: not a ban on tears, a song placed in the hands of the people who'd cry them. Until tomorrow.
